svg.aria-label: Diagram: Amazon EC2 Capacity Manager adds real-time supportability checks and capacity fulfillment metrics. The supportability check is forward-looking and scores how well each instance type and Availability Zone can support a request without launching or reserving instances, returning a High, Medium or Low score for each option plus an overall score. AWS states that a check reflects capacity at a point in time and that it does not reserve capacity or guarantee that a later launch will succeed, so the score is a probability statement rather than an allocation; an On-Demand Capacity Reservation is what actually secures capacity. Capacity fulfillment metrics are backward-looking and show how much capacity was delivered against the amount requested, measurable across the AWS organization, accounts, Regions and tagged workloads with a breakdown by instance type and Availability Zone. Both capabilities are included with AWS Unified Operations, the AWS Support plan, which the documentation states twice as an availability restriction. Three further constraints: Capacity Manager can be enabled in only one AWS Region per account, displayed costs are estimates based on published On-Demand pricing and exclude Savings Plans and Reserved Instance discounts, and the results of supportability checks cannot be shared with third parties.
svg.title: A forecast and a measurement, and neither one is an allocation
svg.text: A High score is not a reservation.
EC2 Capacity Manager — supportability checks and fulfillment metrics.
BEFORE — supportability check
“scoring how well each instance type and Availability
Zone can support a request”
High · Medium · Low + an overall score
Free to run: “without launching or reserving instances”.
AFTER — fulfillment metrics
“how much capacity was delivered against the amount
requested”
Across organization, accounts, Regions and tagged
workloads, by instance type and Availability Zone.
Says how much arrived. Not why.
And the sentence that defines what a score is
“A check reflects capacity at a point in time. It doesn’t reserve capacity or guarantee that a later
launch will succeed.” An On-Demand Capacity Reservation is the thing that allocates.
The last line of the announcement is an eligibility gate, not an availability note
“Both capabilities are included with AWS Unified Operations” — the docs repeat it, in bold, once per capability.
Three constraints to know before planning around it
1. “You can only enable Capacity Manager in one AWS Region per account.” Other Regions aggregate into it.
2. Costs shown are estimates on published On-Demand pricing and “don’t include discounts such as Savings
Plans or Reserved Instances” — an upper bound, never spend.
3. “You can’t share the results of real-time supportability checks with third parties.”
Start with the retrospective number, not the forecast.
Fulfillment rate tells you whether you have a capacity problem. The score is only worth acting on once you
know you do — and its value is showing where adding flexibility would move the overall result.
Record the date beside any score you put in a document. A score without one is a claim the docs do not support.
